q: To maintain concrete consistency, the slump shall be from ____ and shall be determined in accordance with ASTM C143.
n: Structural concrete slump is typically specified at 50–100 mm, tested per ASTM C143. Source: DPWH Standard Specifications, Item 405; ASTM C143.

q: Concrete shall be conveyed from the mixer to the forms as rapidly and as practicable by proper methods. At any point during the conveying, the free vertical drop of the concrete shall not exceed ____ millimeters.
n: Specifications limit the free vertical drop of concrete to prevent segregation, commonly to about 1.2–1.5 m. The item's clause sets 1,200 mm, with chutes or tremies beyond that. Source: ACI 304R (Guide for Measuring, Mixing, Transporting and Placing Concrete); DPWH Standard Specifications, Item 405.

q: All concrete shall be compacted with high-frequency mechanical vibrating equipment supplemented by hand spading and tamping except for concrete slabs of _____ millimeters or less in depth.
n: Concrete is compacted with mechanical vibrators, except thin slabs (100 mm or less), which are consolidated by spading, tamping and screeding. Source: ACI 309R (Guide for Consolidation of Concrete); DPWH Item 405.

q: In general, construction joints in concrete slabs are located ___ of the span.
n: Slab construction joints are located within the middle third of the span, where shear is low. Source: ACI 301; NSCP 2015, Sec. 426.5.6.

q: When is curing most critical?
n: Curing is most critical in the first week (about 7 days), when early hydration builds most of the strength and moisture loss causes cracking. Source: ACI 308R (Guide to Curing Concrete); NSCP 2015, Sec. 426.5.3.

q: How deep should a control joint be sawn in a 4-in. slab on grade?
n: A control joint is sawn to about one quarter of the slab depth: about 1 in. for a 4-in. slab. Source: ACI 302.1R; ACI 224.3R.

q: What makes up about 60–80% of concrete and keeps its cost down?
n: Aggregates make up about 60–80% of concrete's volume and keep its cost down. Source: PCA, Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures.

q: What can replace loose rebars in large slabs on grade poured with ready-mix?
n: Welded wire mesh (fabric) can replace loose bars in large slabs on grade and speeds placement. Source: ACI 360R (Design of Slabs-on-Ground).

q: Concrete is stronger and more durable when the water–cement ratio is:
n: Lower water–cement ratios give stronger, more durable, less porous concrete (Abrams' law). Source: PCA, Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures.

q: Which cement hardens slowest?
n: Portland pozzolan cement gains strength more slowly than ordinary or high-early cement, because pozzolans react slowly. Source: PCA, Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures; ASTM C595.

q: Which admixture speeds early strength gain?
n: An accelerator speeds setting and early strength gain. Calcium chloride is a classic accelerator, but it is limited in reinforced concrete because it promotes corrosion. Source: ASTM C494 (Type C admixtures); PCA.

q: What hard, inert materials such as sand and gravel are added to cement paste for concrete or mortar?
n: Aggregates are the hard, inert materials (sand, gravel, crushed stone) mixed with cement paste to make concrete or mortar. Source: PCA, Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures.

q: Which is NOT a basic requirement of a concrete mix?
n: A concrete mix must give strength, durability, workability and economy. Flexibility is not a requirement, because concrete is rigid. Source: PCA, Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures.

q: What substance, other than cement, water or aggregate, is added to change concrete's properties?
n: An admixture is any material other than cement, water and aggregate added to change concrete's properties. Source: ASTM C125; PCA.

q: What is the minimum strength of Class A concrete?
n: Class A (1:2:4) is the standard structural mix, commonly specified for about 3,000–3,500 psi (21–24 MPa). Of the choices, 3,500 psi is its upper range. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate, Table 1-2 (mix classes); DPWH Item 405.

q: A 1 : 2.5 : 5 mix is:
n: In Fajardo's table, 1:2½:5 is Class B, which uses 7.5 bags of 40 kg cement per m³. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate, Table 1-2.

q: What strength does a 1 : 2.5 : 5 mix give?
n: Class B (1:2½:5) is commonly taken in local practice at about 3,000 psi, a step below Class A. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate, Table 1-2; Philippine practice.

q: What is the mix proportion of Class AA concrete?
n: Class AA concrete uses a 1:1½:3 mix with 12.0 bags of 40 kg cement per m³. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate, Table 1-2.

q: Where should ready-mix concrete be sampled for testing?
n: Ready-mix concrete is sampled on site, at the point of discharge or placement, for slump and cylinder tests. Source: ASTM C172 (Sampling Freshly Mixed Concrete).

q: What water should be used in concrete?
n: Mixing water should be potable, free of oils, acids and organic matter that affect strength or corrode steel. Source: ASTM C1602; NSCP 2015, Sec. 426.4.

q: What is the most important factor affecting the strength of concrete?
n: Water content, through the water–cement ratio, is the most important factor affecting concrete strength (Abrams' law). Source: PCA, Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures.

q: Which test checks the consistency of fresh concrete?
n: The slump test (ASTM C143) checks the consistency of fresh concrete. A cone of fresh concrete is filled, lifted away, and the drop in height (slump) is measured. Source: ASTM C143.

q: Which test measures concrete strength?
n: Concrete strength is measured by compression tests on cylinders (ASTM C39). Standard cylinders are crushed in a testing machine at 7 and 28 days to find f'c. Source: ASTM C39.

q: Class A concrete is NOT needed for:
n: Class A is for structural members (beams, slabs, footings). Footpaths and walks take Class C. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate.

q: What is a typical strength for structural concrete members?
n: Structural concrete members are typically about 3,000 psi (≈21 MPa) or more. Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 419.2.1.

q: What temporary structure, with forms, supports, bracing and hardware, holds fresh concrete?
n: Formwork is the temporary structure (forms, supports, bracing, hardware) that holds fresh concrete until it hardens. Source: ACI 347 (Guide to Formwork for Concrete).

q: Which property of fresh concrete is the effort needed to compact it fully without bleeding or segregation?
n: Workability is the ease of placing and fully compacting fresh concrete without bleeding or segregation. Source: ACI 116R; PCA.

q: What are tiny bubbles deliberately added to cement paste?
n: Entrained air is microscopic bubbles deliberately added with an admixture for freeze-thaw durability and workability. Source: ASTM C260; PCA.

q: What type of concrete has a very low water-cement ratio and is typically used for binding or base layers?
n: Lean concrete is a low-cement mix used for blinding (mud mats) and base layers under footings and slabs. It is defined by low cement content, so the stem's "low w/c" wording is loose. Source: PCA, Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures; ACI 116R.

q: What is the binder in concrete?
n: Cement is the binder. Its paste with water binds the aggregates. Source: PCA, Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures.

q: Which concrete has built-in stresses to counteract tension?
n: Prestressed concrete has built-in compressive stresses that counteract tension from service loads. Source: NSCP 2015, Chapter 4 (prestressed concrete).

q: What device anchors tendons in prestressing?
n: An anchorage device holds the prestressing tendon and transfers its force to the concrete. Source: Post-Tensioning Institute; NSCP 2015.

q: Which test determines concrete strength?
n: Concrete strength is determined by compression testing of cylinders. Standard 150 × 300 mm cylinders, cured and crushed per ASTM C39, give the 28-day compressive strength. Source: ASTM C39.

q: Compared with under-reinforced concrete, over-reinforced concrete is:
n: Over-reinforced concrete fails suddenly by concrete crushing before the steel yields, without warning, so it is more dangerous than ductile under-reinforced concrete. Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 421.2.2 (tension-controlled sections).

q: What is curing?
o: Keeping moisture in so hydration continues
n: Curing keeps moisture (and suitable temperature) in the concrete so hydration continues. Source: ACI 308R.

q: Where are concrete cylinder tests done?
n: Concrete cylinders are tested in an accredited laboratory. Source: ASTM C39; DPWH quality control rules.

q: What is the slump test for?
n: The slump test measures consistency (workability), not strength, sand content or exact water–cement ratio, so "none of the above" is correct. Source: ASTM C143.
